analysis.one_liner: Limits the consumer bureau's power to penalize abusive and deceptive financial practices.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 22 House Republicans, never received a committee vote or floor action and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the consumer bureau's (CFPB's) main enforcement tool against mistreatment of borrowers and account holders. It would have narrowed the definition of an "abusive" practice to require intentional deception, barred the bureau from treating discrimination as abusive, let companies escape monetary penalties by claiming they tried in good faith to follow the law, and given self-reporting companies 180 days to fix violations before enforcement. It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, mortgage lenders, payday and auto lenders, and debt collectors would gain if it passed: they would face a narrower definition of "abusive" conduct, could avoid monetary penalties by showing a good-faith effort to comply, could fix self-reported problems within 180 days before the bureau acts, and would be shielded from civil penalties for conduct before their most recent compliance rating. Firms would also get enforcement cases heard in their headquarters' district or in Washington, D.C. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits_short: Banks, lenders, credit card issuers, debt collectors

how_it_helps.text: Gives companies a shield against monetary penalties if they can show, by a preponderance of the evidence, that they made a good-faith effort to comply with the law, even after the CFPB finds an unfair, deceptive, or abusive practice.

Raises the bar for what counts as 'abusive': the CFPB could only act where a company intentionally and materially interfered with a consumer's understanding of a product's terms, replacing a broader, more flexible standard.
Bars the CFPB from treating discriminatory practices as abusive, an enforcement theory the bureau had begun to use.

Lets a company that self-identifies a problem get written notice and 180 days to cure it before the bureau can take other legal action, and stops the clock on the statute of limitations while that runs.

Prohibits the CFPB from seeking civil money penalties for conduct that occurred before a company's most recent compliance rating, and requires cost-benefit analysis before any new rule on unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who are misled, pressured, or discriminated against by financial companies would bear the cost: fewer monetary penalties against firms, harder cases to bring where harm was not provably intentional, no abusive-practice route for discrimination claims, and civil penalties off the table for older conduct. Consumers recovering money for identifiable harm could still get restitution, but the main deterrent penalties would shrink. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers using loans, cards, and credit

drawbacks.text: A company that deceived or confused customers could avoid monetary penalties simply by convincing a court it tried in good faith to comply, weakening the main financial consequence of mistreating consumers.
Discrimination in consumer finance could no longer be challenged as an abusive practice, removing one enforcement route for borrowers facing discriminatory treatment.

Requiring that interference with a consumer's understanding be both intentional and material would let companies escape liability for fine print, bait-and-switch terms, or confusion they caused without provable intent.
The look-back provision would bar civil penalties for conduct preceding a company's most recent compliance rating, wiping out penalty exposure for older violations.

Supporters' strongest argument is that the original 'abusive' standard was vague and gave regulators room to second-guess ordinary products; the bill would have added clarity, but its good-faith shield, cure rights, and penalty look-back go well beyond clarification and reduce money flowing back to harmed consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered financial firms real legal certainty and protection from penalties, and the case for clarifying a genuinely vague standard is legitimate. But the specific remedies went far beyond clarity: a good-faith escape from monetary penalties, 180-day cure rights, and a penalty look-back would have cut the money consumers recover and the deterrent companies face, while carving discrimination out of the abusive standard entirely. The costs to consumers outweighed the clarity benefit.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2023, sent to the House Financial Services Committee, and sat there with no markup, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services the same day.
Twenty-one House Republicans signed on as cosponsors, joining Barr, for 22 Republican backers in total and no Democratic support.
The committee took no further action on the bill for the remaining thirteen months of the Congress, and it never received a House vote.
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, leaving the CFPB's existing unfair, deceptive, and abusive practices authority unchanged.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers are better off because the bill died: the CFPB keeps its current power to penalize companies for unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices, including for discrimination and for conduct a company claims was a good-faith mistake.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Consumers and the CFPB's enforcement authority

for.name: Rep. Andy Barr
for.role: U.S. Representative (R-KY), bill sponsor; chair of the Financial Services subcommittee on financial institutions
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, to narrow the CFPB's abusive-practice standard and add good-faith, cure, and penalty-look-back protections for financial firms.

for.name: Banks and consumer lenders
for.what_they_did: Have long pushed to narrow the CFPB's 'abusive' standard and limit monetary penalties; the bill's provisions track those industry asks.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee (Chair Patrick McHenry)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill during the thirteen months it sat in committee, keeping it off the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 22 sponsors and cosponsors were House Republicans and no Democrat signed on; because the bill never reached a vote, there is no roll-call record of where the full chamber stood.

industries.note: The bill would have narrowed the standard used to police their dealings with borrowers, barred monetary penalties when they claim good-faith compliance, and wiped out penalty exposure for pre-rating conduct. Consumers would get fewer penalties paid on their behalf and weaker deterrence.

industries.industry: Credit card issuers, payday and auto lenders, and debt collectors
industries.note: These firms are frequent targets of CFPB enforcement over confusing terms and aggressive collection. Requiring intentional, material deception and allowing a 180-day cure window would have made cases against them much harder to bring.

The bill would have stripped the bureau of tools it uses to win monetary relief: the flexible abusive standard, alternative legal claims, penalty look-back, and discrimination-as-abusive theory. The bureau's interest here runs with consumers', since enforcement recovers money for them.
